title: Nucleus: Discovery of Nucleus
notes: Atomic Models Timeline: Dalton's solid sphere (1808) → Thomson's plum pudding (1897) → Rutherford's nuclear model (1911) → Bohr's quantum model (1913). Each model addressed limitations of the previous.
Thomson's Plum Pudding Model: Atom as positively charged pudding with electrons embedded like plums. Could not explain alpha scattering results.

Rutherford's Alpha Scattering Experiment: Alpha particles from radioactive source directed at thin gold foil (~0.00004 cm). Most passed straight, some deflected at small angles, very few (~1 in 8000) bounced back at angles >90°.

Rutherford's Nuclear Model: Atom has tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (~10⁻¹⁴ m) containing nearly all mass. Electrons revolve around nucleus at large distance (~10⁻¹⁰ m). Most of atom is empty space.
Nuclear Size: Nuclear radius R ≈ R₀A^(1/3) where R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm (10⁻¹⁵ m) and A is mass number. Nucleus is ~10⁴ times smaller than atom.
Nuclear Composition: Nucleus contains protons (Z = atomic number) and neutrons (N = neutron number). Mass number A = Z + N. Nucleus charge = +Ze.
Limitations of Rutherford Model: Could not explain atomic stability (accelerating electrons should radiate energy and spiral into nucleus) or line spectra.
specificConditions: Alpha Particle Source: Rutherford used alpha particles (helium nuclei, +2e charge, ~5 MeV energy) from radioactive decay (radium/polonium).
Thin Foil: Gold foil used because gold is highly malleable — can be made extremely thin (~400 atoms thick) so alpha particles interact with at most one atom.
Point Charge Approximation: Alpha particle treated as point charge; nucleus treated as point charge — valid since distances are much larger than nuclear/alpha sizes.
formulas: Impact parameter: $b$ — perpendicular distance of initial velocity from nucleus center
Scattering angle: $\theta$ — related to impact parameter $b$ and energy
Closest approach: $d = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{2Ze^2}{K}$ for head-on collision (K = alpha kinetic energy)
keyPoints: Rutherford's experiment revealed tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus.
Most alpha particles passed through gold foil — atom is mostly empty space.
Few bounced back — concentrated positive charge in nucleus.
Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3), R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm.
Nucleus contains Z protons and N neutrons; A = Z + N.
importantStatements: Statement 1: Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment established the nuclear model of the atom.
Statement 2: The nucleus is ~10⁻¹⁴ m in diameter, contains nearly all atomic mass and positive charge.
Statement 3: Most of the atom is empty space — electrons orbit at ~10⁻¹⁰ m from nucleus.
Statement 4: Nuclear radius follows R = R₀A^(1/3) with R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm.
Statement 5: Rutherford model could not explain atomic stability or line spectra.
importantNotes: Only ~1 in 8000 alpha particles scattered by >90° — evidence of tiny nucleus.
Gold foil chosen for malleability (can be made atomically thin).
Impact parameter determines scattering angle — smaller b → larger deflection.
Distance of closest approach estimates upper limit of nuclear size.
examShortTricks: Most passed straight → atom mostly empty.
Few deflected → small concentrated positive charge.
Very few bounced back → head-on collision with massive nucleus.
Nucleus is 10⁴ times smaller than atom.
R = R₀A^(1/3) for nuclear size estimation.
examNotes: NEB frequently asks to describe Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment and draw conclusions.
Distance of closest approach calculation is a standard numerical.
Limitations of Rutherford model (stability, spectra) lead to Bohr model.
Alpha particle properties: +2e charge, helium nucleus, ~5 MeV energy.
examples: Alpha particle (K = 5.5 MeV) head-on with gold nucleus (Z = 79): d = (9×10⁹)(2×79×(1.6×10⁻¹⁹)²)/(5.5×10⁶×1.6×10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m.
If atom were size of football stadium, nucleus would be size of a marble at center.

universalFacts: Rutherford's gold foil experiment (1911) is considered one of the most important experiments in physics history.
The term 'nucleus' was coined by Rutherford in 1912.
Geiger and Marsden were the students who actually performed the experiment under Rutherford's direction.
The backscattering fraction (~1/8000) was so surprising Rutherford said it was like 'firing a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and having it bounce back'.
confusion: Confusing Thomson and Rutherford models: Thomson = positive pudding with electrons; Rutherford = tiny nucleus with electrons orbiting.
Thinking nucleus contains electrons: Nucleus contains only protons and neutrons (neutrons discovered later by Chadwick, 1932).
Believing all alpha particles bounce back: Only ~1/8000 scatter >90°; most pass through.
Confusing nuclear size with atomic size: Nucleus ~10⁻¹⁴ m, atom ~10⁻¹⁰ m — factor of 10⁴ difference.
Thinking Rutherford model explains spectra: It cannot explain line spectra or atomic stability.

mcs.question: In Rutherford's experiment, most alpha particles:
mcs.explanation: Atom is mostly empty space — most alpha particles pass without interaction.

mcs.question: The nucleus contains nearly all the:
mcs.explanation: Protons and neutrons in nucleus account for ~99.97% of atomic mass.

mcs.question: Nuclear radius is proportional to:
mcs.explanation: R = R₀A^(1/3) — radius proportional to cube root of mass number.

mcs.question: Alpha particle has charge:
mcs.explanation: Alpha particle is helium nucleus: 2 protons, charge +2e.

mcs.question: Distance of closest approach for head-on collision:
mcs.explanation: d ∝ 1/K — higher energy alpha penetrates closer to nucleus.

summary: Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment revealed a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (~10⁻¹⁴ m) containing nearly all atomic mass. Most of the atom is empty space. Nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3). Rutherford's model could not explain stability or spectra — leading to Bohr's quantum model.
